note: Hand-curated from cmfclearinghouse.fhwa.dot.gov with every sourceUrl opened on the lastReviewed date. Rows without a factor are deliberate: nothing at 3 stars or better isolates that treatment, and shipping a weak number would be worse than shipping none. CMFs are national averages, never promises about a specific corner.

interventions.study: Goughnour et al. 2018, Safety Evaluation of Protected Left-Turn Phasing and Leading Pedestrian Intervals on Pedestrian Safety
interventions.notes: Five-star empirical study across Chicago, New York, Charlotte and Toronto. The strongest factor in this table.

interventions.study: Empirical Bayesian evaluation of high-visibility (yellow) school crosswalks in San Francisco
interventions.notes: Four stars, and the study city is San Francisco itself, but the sites were school zones with yellow markings; white continental crosswalks at a transit intersection are a related, not identical, treatment. The two-star general urban study (facid 4123, CMF 0.6) was rejected for quality. This is the conservative, higher-CMF survivor.
No high-quality published factor. Clearinghouse entries that include curb extensions bundle them inside road-diet packages, so no factor of 3 stars or better isolates the treatment.

No high-quality published factor. Parking-restriction CMFs on the clearinghouse are compendium entries without empirical star ratings (e.g. facid 1786). San Francisco's own California Street evaluation, which included daylighting, appears on the precedents table instead.

No high-quality published factor. The separated-bike-lane rows from Rothenberg et al. 2016 (facids 8232, 8248, 8287) carry one star, and the opened 8248 row shows a CMF above 1.0, which says more about the data than the treatment. FHWA published a 2023 separated-bike-lane CMF study not yet star-rated on the clearinghouse at review time.
